concepts.def: The first stage of development: defining the problem precisely, gathering requirements and producing a specification of what the solution must do.
Planning the solution before coding: choosing data structures and algorithms, and designing the modules, interfaces and tests to be used.
Writing the actual program code from the design, typically building and combining modules and refining them as work proceeds.
Running the program with selected data, including normal, boundary and erroneous values, to detect errors and confirm requirements are met.
Judging how well the finished solution meets the requirements and criteria from analysis, and identifying possible improvements.
Building simplified working versions of a system early so users can give feedback that refines the requirements and design.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Systematic Approach To Problem Solving — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Systematic Approach To Problem Solving brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Systematic Approach To Problem Solving.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The first stage in a systematic approach to problem solving is:
options: Analysis - defining the problem and its requirements
Writing all the program code
Marketing the finished product
Deleting old software
Planned algorithms, data structures and interface designs, before coding begins
The final boxed product
Only the user manual
A list of competitors

mcqs.q: The main purpose of testing is to:
options: Find errors and check the solution meets its requirements
Prove mathematically that no bugs can exist
Make the code run more slowly
Replace the analysis stage

mcqs.q: Evaluation involves judging the solution against:
options: The requirements and criteria established during analysis
The personal taste of one programmer
The number of lines of code written
The age of the computer used

mcqs.q: Should testing wait until the whole program is finished?
options: Yes - testing before completion always gives meaningless results.
Yes - testing is a single final stage after all coding is complete.
No - testing should happen iteratively as each module is built, so errors are found early when they are cheapest and easiest to fix.
Yes - analysis means choosing the colour scheme first.

mcqs.q: Is analysis just starting to write the code straight away?
options: Yes - evaluation is just running the tests a second time.
Yes - analysis means choosing the colour scheme first.
Yes - the fastest start is to begin typing code immediately.
No - analysis defines the problem and requirements before any code is written; coding without analysis risks building the wrong solution entirely.

mcqs.q: Are testing and evaluation the same activity?
options: Yes - evaluation is just running the tests a second time.
Yes - testing before completion always gives meaningless results.
Yes - once the tests pass, evaluation has automatically happened.
No - testing finds errors and checks behaviour, while evaluation judges the overall solution against requirements and criteria, including usability and efficiency.
